----------------------------------------------------------------
Empirical Research Plan
----------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
   • Method: Difference-in-Differences (panel fixed-effects) with a continuous “treatment” (weather shocks).  
   • Rationale:  
     – Weather in a given county-year is plausibly random after conditioning on county and year fixed effects; hence within-county deviations from the long-run mean serve as exogenous shocks.  
     – A two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) specification is algebraically identical to a DID that compares “treated” (unusually hot/dry/wet) county-years with “control” (normal-weather) county-years, netting out time-invariant county factors and nationwide shocks.  
     – The continuous-treatment DID easily accommodates heterogeneous intensities (e.g., degree-days, inches of rainfall).  
     – This framework naturally extends to an event-study (dynamic) specification to verify pre-trends and persistence.

2. Treatment and Control  
   • Treatment variable: Weather anomaly in county c, year t, defined as  
          TempAnom_ct  =  Growing-season average temperature – county-specific 1950-2000 mean  
          PrecAnom_ct  =  Growing-season total precipitation – county-specific mean  
     We will also construct:  
          GDD_ct = Σ max(0, Temp_day – 10 °C) below 29 °C  
          HDD_ct = Σ max(0, Temp_day – 29 °C) (extreme heat)  
   • “Treated” observations: County-years with non-zero anomalies; intensity is continuous.  
   • Control group: The same counties in years when anomalies ≈ 0 (or, in robustness, anomalies within the inter-quartile range).  
   • Timing: Annual; treatment varies every year. No single “event date” is required.  
   • No running variable & cutoff (not RDD).

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
   A1. Conditional exogeneity: After conditioning on county FE, year FE, and controls, weather shocks are uncorrelated with unobserved determinants of yield.  
        – Plausible because daily weather is driven by atmospheric physics, not farm decisions.  
   A2. Parallel trends (in expectation): In the absence of weather shocks, yield growth in treated and control county-years would have been the same.  
        – Plausible once county FE, year FE, and county-specific linear time trends are included.  
   A3. No spatial spillovers that violate SUTVA: A weather shock in county c does not directly change yield in neighboring county c′ except through its own weather (which is observed).  
        – Reasonable at county scale; we will cluster SEs by agricultural-climate region to be safe.  
   A4. Stable production technology within short windows: Year-to-year technological progress is absorbed by year FE; longer-run adaptation is handled with county trends.  
        – Plausible for annual shocks.

4. Threats to Identification & Remedies  
   1. Measurement error in weather or yields → Attenuation bias.  
        • Use PRISM/NOAA gridded weather reanalysis matched to counties to improve precision.  
        • Instrument extreme-heat days (HDD) with neighboring-county weather as a Berkson-type IV robustness check.  
   2. Adaptive input choices endogenously respond to expected weather (e.g., irrigation).  
        • Focus on unexpected shocks (deviation from 10-day forecasts) in robustness.  
        • Control for irrigation coverage, fertilizer price, crop insurance penetration (from USDA Census, interpolated).  
   3. Spatial autocorrelation & serial correlation of errors → Under-estimated standard errors.  
        • Cluster at the 9 NOAA climate-region × state level (≈ 40 clusters) and apply Conley (1999) spatial HAC in robustness.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# ----------------------------------------------------
# 0. Load packages
# ----------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)    # fast data handling
library(fixest)        # high-performance FE regressions
library(lmtest)        # coeftest for clustering
library(sandwich)      # variance-covariance estimators
library(modelsummary)  # nice tables

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# ----------------------------------------------------
yield  <- fread("usda_county_yield_1950_2000.csv")     # county, year, crop yields
weather <- fread("county_daily_weather_1950_2000.csv") # county, date, temp, precip

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# ----------------------------------------------------
# Aggregate daily weather to growing-season (Apr–Sep) stats
weather[, `:=`(
  gdd = pmax(temp - 10, 0)][temp < 29, sum(gdd), by=.(county, year)],  # GDD
  hdd = pmax(temp - 29, 0)][, sum(hdd), by=.(county, year)],            # HDD
  precip_gs = sum(precip),                                              # rainfall
  temp_gs   = mean(temp)                                                # avg temp
), by = .(county, year)]

# Merge
dt <- merge(yield, weather, by = c("county","year"))

# Long-run county means (1950-2000)
dt[, `:=`(
  temp_bar  = mean(temp_gs), 
  precip_bar= mean(precip_gs)
), by = county]

# Weather anomalies
dt[, `:=`(
  temp_anom  = temp_gs   - temp_bar,
  precip_anom= precip_gs - precip_bar
)]

# Log yields (example with corn)
dt[, lnyld_corn := log(corn_yield)]

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main specification: TWFE DID
# ----------------------------------------------------
main <- feols(
  lnyld_corn ~ temp_anom + I(temp_anom^2) + precip_anom + I(precip_anom^2) + 
               gdd + hdd | county + year + county:trend,
  data = dt,
  cluster = ~county
)
etable(main, se = "cluster")

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: event-study around extreme heat years
# ----------------------------------------------------
# Define extreme-heat event
dt[, extreme_heat := as.integer(hdd > quantile(hdd, 0.9)), by = county]

# Leads/lags (-3…+3 years)
for (k in -3:3) dt[, paste0("L",k,"_ext") := shift(extreme_heat, n = k, type = "lag"), by = county]

leadlag_vars <- paste0("L", -3:3, "_ext")[ -4 ] # drop k=0 to avoid collinearity
formula_event <- as.formula(
  paste("lnyld_corn ~", paste(leadlag_vars, collapse = " + "), "| county + year")
)

event <- feols(formula_event, data = dt, cluster = ~county)
iplot(event, ref.line = 0)

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 5. Spatial-HAC SEs (Conley) as robustness
# ----------------------------------------------------
# Use fixest::coeftest with vcov = vcov_conley if desired
conley_se <- vcov_conley(main, lat = ~lat, lon = ~lon, cutoff = 500e3)
coeftest(main, vcov = conley_se)
```

6. Expected Results  
   • Direction:  
     – Higher extreme heat (HDD) should lower yields; moderate GDD should raise yields.  
     – Additional precipitation benefits yields up to a point; too much causes losses (inverted-U).  
   • Magnitude (based on agronomic literature):  
     – Corn: 1 additional °C in average growing-season temperature (holding rain constant) → ~5-8 % lower yield.  
     – Each additional inch of precipitation up to the 75th percentile → ~1 % higher yield; beyond that, diminishing or negative.  
   • Climate change projection: A +2 °C scenario with unchanged precipitation would reduce average corn yields ~10–15 %.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
   (1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)

   C1. Parallel trends plausibly hold after fixed effects & trends …………………… 0.8  
   C2. No interference between units (SUTVA) ………………………………………… 0.7  
   C3. Exogenous treatment assignment (weather shocks) …………………………… 0.9  
   C4. No differential measurement error across treatment/control ……………… 0.8  
   C5. Correct functional form & absence of dynamic bias …………………………… 0.7  

   Average score ≈ 0.78 → Method appears credible but still warrants robustness tests described above.

----------------------------------------------------------------
